question: Does a term get its name in a sentence that exists only to announce the name, in a fixed shape the piece uses again for other terms? Flag each such naming sentence from the second use of the shape onward.

Do three or more sentences or paragraphs in different parts of the piece begin with the same connective move, so that the opening reads as a habit and not as a link the thought needed? Flag each one after the second.
Is there a run of two or more very short sentences or fragments placed for the beat they make, where the thought they carry is not itself short and could have been one plain sentence? Flag the run.

Does a sentence hold back its point for a reveal after a colon or dash, or hand over a list of exactly three items chosen for rhythm, where a plain statement would have said the same? Flag the sentence.

Is there a simile or 'it is like' comparison that only tells the reader what the thing resembles, and from which the reader could not work anything out about how it behaves? Flag it. A comparison the piece then reasons from is not a hit.
Does a paragraph or the piece end on a short line shaped to be quoted, which restates or moralises what was already said and adds no step, fact or reason? Flag the line.
Does a sentence promise or withhold something (what is coming next, how many points there will be, a reveal later) where the piece could simply have said the thing? Flag it.
Is there a recap made of several short clauses or sentences built to the same pattern, one per thing covered? Flag the recap.

Does the piece state a causal or surprising claim as a bare fact and move on, at a point where its own subject offered a step, a number or a case that would have shown it? Flag the claim. A claim the piece goes on to show is not a hit.

Do three or more consecutive paragraphs have the same build (the same number of sentences in the same roles, ending the same way)? Flag the first sentence of each paragraph in the run after the first.
Is a term given as the answer or the fix before the reader has been shown the thing it names, so that the name arrives with nothing to attach it to? Flag the sentence.

Does a sentence build up to a reveal, or tell the reader that things are about to get interesting, strange or surprising, when what follows is an ordinary point of the explanation? Flag the build-up sentence.

Does a sentence announce that something is about to be said, or tell the reader what the piece is going to do, in place of saying or doing it? Flag it. A signpost that tells a listener where they are in a long spoken piece is not a hit.
Is a question asked only so the writer can answer it in the next few words, where the reader would not have been asking it at that point? Flag the question together with its answer.

Is a plain claim set up as a correction of a view that nobody in the piece holds and the reader is unlikely to hold, so that it sounds like an insight? Flag the sentence. Correcting a misconception that people really have, and that the piece explains, is not a hit.
Is the reader told that something is fascinating, remarkable, surprising, elegant or important, where the piece could have shown the thing and let it be so? Flag the telling.
Is an ordinary subject framed as world-changing, or a detail as the key to everything? Flag the sentence.
Is there a sentence that could appear unchanged in a piece on a different subject, because it contains no number, name, mechanism or case from this one? Flag it.

Is there an example with placeholder actors and no concrete detail a reader could check or picture (no name, number, place or outcome), at a point where the subject offers a specific one? Flag the example.
Does a sentence or short passage introduce two or more technical terms without saying what each does before moving on? Flag the passage.

Could the opening sentence or two introduce a piece on almost any subject, because it works by a stock move (an invitation to imagine, a claim that most people do not know something, a promise to overturn what the reader thinks) and not by anything about this subject? Flag it.
Does the piece narrate its own guiding of the reader (inviting them to come along, to get ready, to stay with it) in place of explaining? Flag the sentence.
Does the final line turn the content into a moral, a slogan or an instruction to the reader about their own life? Flag it.
